scope.flow: FlashAccountant.updateDebt() debt mutation during an active lock, reached via a native ETH withdrawal callback to a malicious recipient contract
evidence: FlashAccountant.updateDebt() lacks locker authorization, allowing malicious ETH recipients to brick their own locks
src/base/FlashAccountant.sol – updateDebt()
updateDebt() uses _getLocker() instead of _requireLocker() to obtain the active lock.

Because updateDebt() is external and only uses _getLocker(), any contract that is called while a lock is active can invoke updateDebt() and inject arbitrary debt for the current lock, even though it is not the locker.

One concrete and realistic path is through native ETH withdrawals: when a locker calls withdraw() with the native token and a recipient address, the FlashAccountant does a low-level call to that recipient. If the recipient is a contract with a receive() function, that receive() runs while the lock is still active and can call updateDebt().
In FlashAccountant.updateDebt():
uint256 id = _getLocker().id();  // <-- no msg.sender == locker check
_accountDebt(id, msg.sender, delta);
This inconsistency means that updateDebt() is the only debt-mutating public interface that does not enforce msg.sender == locker.addr().

statements.text: updateDebt() obtains the active lock via _getLocker(), which only checks that a lock is active and does not verify msg.sender is the current locker, unlike _requireLocker() used by other debt-mutating entrypoints.
evidence: updateDebt() uses _getLocker() instead of _requireLocker() to obtain the active lock.
_getLocker() only checks that a lock is active.
_requireLocker() additionally enforces that msg.sender is the current locker.
uint256 id = _getLocker().id();  // <-- no msg.sender == locker check
_getLocker() only ensures a lock exists; it does not verify that the caller is the current locker.
This inconsistency means that updateDebt() is the only debt-mutating public interface that does not enforce msg.sender == locker.addr().

statements.text: Only the current locker (msg.sender == locker.addr()) should be able to mutate the active lock's debt through debt-mutating public entrypoints such as updateDebt().
evidence: _requireLocker() additionally enforces that msg.sender is the current locker.
By contrast, other public entrypoints that mutate debt (e.g. withdraw()) use _requireLocker(), which does:
if (locker.addr() != msg.sender) revert LockerOnly();  // proper auth check
This inconsistency means that updateDebt() is the only debt-mutating public interface that does not enforce msg.sender == locker.addr().

statements.text: At the end of a lock, the DebtsNotZeroed invariant should hold so that a lock completes without injected non-zero debt causing a revert.
evidence: Injected debt increments the per-lock non-zero debt counter, so when the lock completes, the final DebtsNotZeroed check fails and the whole operation reverts.
Cause the lock to always fail its DebtsNotZeroed invariant at the end of execution.
The fake debt increments the lock’s non-zero debt counter, which is checked at the end of the lock, causing DebtsNotZeroed and reverting the entire transaction.

ambiguities: Report states all ETH recipients in existing code paths are user-controlled, so the scenario is self-DoS/griefing of one's own operation rather than cross-user griefing; the victim/locker and attacker roles overlap.
The report does not establish a prior transaction or pre-existing debt state; the injected debt is produced by the checked action itself.
Whether the malicious recipient is chosen by the locker or by a third party is not established beyond the locker choosing the recipient address.
